summary:
An FMLink article covering a presentation by Dr. Omrana Pasha-Razzak, MD, MSPH, an academic physician and epidemiologist at CUNY, at the ISSA Healthcare Surfaces Summit (dated May 5, 2026), arguing that environmental services (EVS) staff should be formally included in hospital interprofessional care teams.

Core argument: the daily 7:30 a.m. inpatient huddle (attending physician, charge nurse, pharmacist, case manager, social worker) has progressively expanded since the Institute of Medicine's 1999 report To Err is Human, which linked preventable deaths to gaps between clinical silos and called for interprofessional team-based care. Pharmacists, case managers and social workers were each added over time despite resistance, but EVS was never brought in, even though EVS workers spend more minutes in a patient room than nurses or doctors.

Information asymmetry: clinical teams know which rooms have C. diff, MRSA or VRE precautions, which incoming patients are neutropenic and need specific room preparation, and who is being discharged. EVS staff typically learn about isolation precautions only on arrival at the door and learn of discharges when the patient is wheeled out, despite elevated infection risk for patients placed in rooms previously occupied by infected patients.

Patient flow: ED boarding is framed as an economic and mortality issue, with room turnaround time presented as the largest lever after clinical decision-making. Several studies are cited showing turnaround and charge-to-readiness times falling sharply when clinical and EVS communication improves, including walkie-talkie deployment saving boarding hours. Expected discharge date, known from admission, is routinely withheld from EVS until the last moment.

Secondary domain: respiratory risk, where patients admitted for asthma or chronic lung disease may be exposed to cleaning products that worsen symptoms, with the article noting an absence of research literature on this. The piece positions the omission as a structural system failure, not an EVS performance failure.

claims.claim: The person who spends the greatest number of minutes with a patient in their room is the environmental services worker, not a nurse or doctor, yet they are not part of the interprofessional team
claims.attribution: Dr. Omrana Pasha-Razzak, MD, MSPH, CUNY, speaking at the ISSA Healthcare Surfaces Summit

claims.claim: The 1999 Institute of Medicine report To Err is Human documented preventable deaths caused by gaps between clinical silos rather than clinical ignorance
claims.stat: tens of thousands of preventable deaths
claims.attribution: Institute of Medicine (now the National Academy of Medicine), cited in the article

claims.claim: Incoming patients face greater risk of hospital-acquired infection when placed in a room previously occupied by an infected patient
Better communication, rather than more staffing, money or cleaning personnel, drove a drop in C. diff cases on two oncology units when the clinical team shared real-time feedback with EVS workers
Severely ill patients boarded in the emergency department for more than six hours show increased mortality, along with longer ICU stays and higher rates of adverse events
A Lean study found room turnaround time dropped when communication between clinical and environmental teams improved
claims.attribution: Lean study cited in the article

claims.claim: A study tracking charge-to-readiness time recorded a reduction
One hospital found that the majority of delays in outflow from the emergency department were caused by communication failures between the clinical team and EVS
claims.attribution: Hospital study cited in the article

claims.claim: Providing both clinical and EVS teams with walkie-talkies saved boarding time over nine months
There is essentially no research literature on the effects of cleaning products on hospitalized patients with respiratory conditions

vocabulary: To Err is Human: Building a Safer Health System
